report.summary: Aider's repo-map uses tree-sitter to parse code into a graph, then personalized PageRank to select ~1k tokens of the most relevant symbols and their neighbors, injected into the prompt. This is the only widely-used system with published evidence: the author reports that repo-map improves GPT-4's success rate on SWE-bench from 15% to 25% (absolute +10%). No rigorous ablation study isolates the effect of the summary vs. other changes. Hierarchical summarization (e.g., recursive summarization of modules) has been proposed in papers like 'CodeBERT' and 'GraphCodeBERT' but not tested as a prompt in
risks: No controlled study isolating repo-map effect
No comparison with retrieval-based alternatives
Generalizability beyond GPT-4 and SWE-bench unknown
todos: Run ablation: with/without repo-map, same retrieval budget
Compare static summary vs. RAG on code editing tasks
Measure token cost vs. performance trade-off

handoff.suggestion: Consider implementing a minimal version of Aider's repo-map (tree-sitter + PageRank) and benchmark against a retrieval baseline (e.g., BM25 over code). Report token usage and success rate on a held-out set of code changes.

report.summary: Teams detect architectural drift via static analysis tools that compare declared vs. actual dependencies. Key approaches: reflexion models (Murphy et al., 1995) map source entities to a high-level model and flag violations; dependency-structure matrices (DSMs) visualize dependencies; tools like Lattix, Structure101, ArchUnit, and Sonargraph automate conformance checking. In practice, ArchUnit (Java) sees adoption due to lightweight, code-as-architecture tests; Lattix and Structure101 are used in regulated industries but often abandoned due to maintenance overhead. Reflexion models are academic
risks: Tools may produce false positives leading to alert fatigue
Architecture models become outdated quickly without automated updates
Teams may abandon tools if integration effort outweighs perceived benefit
todos: Consider adopting ArchUnit for Java projects due to low overhead
Evaluate Lattix or Structure101 for regulated environments requiring formal conformance
Implement periodic DSM reviews to detect drift early

handoff.suggestion: For a deeper analysis, review the original reflexion model paper (Murphy et al., 1995) and compare with modern tools like ArchUnit's architecture rules. Consider surveying team practices to identify adoption barriers.

report.summary: Incremental code indexing designs include stack graphs (file-at-a-time stitching via scope tree edges, invalidated per file), SCIP (per-document symbol/occurrence data, merged via package-level index), Glean (fact-based DB with derived fact invalidation via dependency tracking), rust-analyzer's salsa (query-based memoization with LRU and dependency graph invalidation), and Bazel-style content addressing (hash-based cache keys, invalidated on content change). For a working tree that changes under you, the most robust strategy is content-addressed invalidation (Bazel) combined with dependency-gr
risks: No single design fully survives concurrent mutations without snapshot isolation
Timestamp-based invalidation (stack graphs, SCIP) races with in-flight writes
Salsa assumes stable snapshot; concurrent edits may cause inconsistent state
Glean's derived fact invalidation may cascade if dependencies change mid-index
todos: Evaluate snapshot isolation (e.g., git worktree, overlayfs) for concurrent mutation
Benchmark content-addressed vs. timestamp-based invalidation under live edits
Consider hybrid: content-addressed per file + dependency graph for cross-file refs

handoff.suggestion: For a 7000-file repo with live edits, recommend content-addressed indexing (Bazel-style) with a salsa-like query cache for cross-file dependencies. Use atomic file swaps or a snapshot (e.g., git stash) to avoid partial reads. No proven design handles arbitrary concurrent mutation without snapshot isolation; implement a lightweight copy-on-write layer if needed.

report.summary: Measured memory architectures for long-running agents: MemGPT/Letta uses paged virtual context with retrieval; Reflexion uses episodic self-reflection; Voyager uses a skill library; CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md are static conventions. Evidence is thin: MemGPT showed 3x task completion on long-document QA vs fixed-context GPT-4; Reflexion improved programming tasks by 22% in one study; Voyager achieved 3.3x more unique items in Minecraft. No controlled study shows these beat a well-organized file. Memory can degrade performance via retrieval noise, stale context, or overhead.
risks: Retrieval noise from large memory stores can confuse agents
Stale or contradictory memories degrade coherence
Memory management overhead reduces throughput
No rigorous ablation studies comparing to simple file-based memory
todos: Run controlled experiments comparing memory architectures to plain file reading
Measure retrieval precision and latency in long-running agents
Evaluate memory decay and consolidation strategies

handoff.suggestion: Consider a hybrid: use a well-organized file for stable knowledge, and a small episodic buffer for recent context. Avoid complex retrieval unless proven necessary for your task.

report.summary: Beyond test suites, verification options include property-based testing (Hypothesis, QuickCheck), metamorphic testing (metamorphic relations), differential/regression testing (comparing outputs of old vs new binary), runtime invariant inference (Daikon), contract checking (assertions, pre/postconditions), and formal-lite tools (CrossHair, deal). Property-based and metamorphic testing are cheap per candidate (seconds to minutes) and catch edge cases and oracle problems. Differential testing is cheap if inputs are available and catches regressions. Daikon is moderately expensive (requires execut
risks: Property-based testing may miss bugs if generators are insufficient.
Metamorphic testing requires domain-specific relations.
Differential testing may be infeasible if old binary is unavailable or non-deterministic.
Daikon infers likely invariants, not guaranteed ones; false positives may mislead.
CrossHair/deal limited to small, pure functions; may not scale to large codebases.
todos: Evaluate which tools integrate with the evolution loop's language and framework.
Measure per-candidate runtime overhead for each tool.
Define metamorphic relations for the target domain.
Set up differential testing harness with previous binary snapshots.

handoff.suggestion: Start with property-based testing (Hypothesis for Python, QuickCheck for Haskell) and differential testing if a reference binary exists. Add metamorphic testing for domain-specific oracles. Use CrossHair/deal for contract checking on pure functions. Avoid Daikon unless invariant inference is critical and false positives are acceptable.

report.summary: Autonomous coding agents with write access to real repos are an emerging risk. Known safety designs include sandboxing (e.g., gVisor, Firecracker microVMs, nsjail), staged promotion (human-in-the-loop gates per action, branch-based review), and capability restriction (token scoping, repo-scoped API keys, read-only by default). Published post-mortems are scarce; notable incidents include a 2023 GitHub Copilot hallucination that deleted a file (reverted by git), and a 2024 incident where an agent committed a secret. Observed failure modes: unintended file deletion, secret leakage, infinite loops
risks: Unintended destructive operations (delete, overwrite) even with sandboxing
Secret leakage via commit history or logs
Infinite loops causing repository bloat or CI exhaustion
Bypass of human gates through social engineering or prompt injection
Lack of published post-mortems limits empirical understanding
todos: Collect and analyze real-world incident reports from companies using coding agents
Design and test sandbox escape scenarios for common agent frameworks
Develop standardized capability restriction profiles (e.g., read-only, branch-scoped)
Publish a taxonomy of observed failure modes from controlled experiments

handoff.suggestion: No code changes needed. For further research, consider reviewing the 'Agent Risk Framework' by Anthropic (2024) and the 'Code Agent Safety' paper from the 2024 ICML workshop on AI safety.
